title: A computer, not a person, decides when Rotterdam's giant storm barrier closes

cover.alt: The Maeslantkering during a test closure: two huge white steel truss arms swinging curved gates across the waterway.

body: The **Maeslantkering**, opened by Queen Beatrix on 10 May 1997 after six years of construction, guards the Nieuwe Waterweg, the shipping channel into Rotterdam. Its two steel gates are 210 m long and 22 m high, each swung by a 237 m truss arm weighing 6,800 tonnes that pivots on a ball joint 10 m across, the largest in the world. Normally the gates rest in dry docks on either bank and ships pass freely. A centralised computer system called **BOS** watches the forecasts, and when a surge of 3 m above the Dutch reference level is expected at Rotterdam it closes the barrier itself: the docks flood, the hollow gates float out across the channel, then fill with water and sink to the bottom of the waterway. It first closed for real on 8 November 2007 and is designed for a storm so severe it occurs only once in 10,000 years.

slides.alt: A ship sailing along the Nieuwe Waterweg past one of the Maeslantkering's open gates resting in its dock.
slides.caption: Open for business: a ship passes while the Maeslantkering's gates rest in their docks on the banks. The barrier is part of the Delta Works, the Netherlands' flood defences.

slides.heading: Maeslantkering sizes, in metres: higher or lower?
slides.explanation: Each gate is 22 m high and 210 m long, swung by a 237 m truss arm on a ball joint 10 m across.

slides.label: weight of each ball joint, the world's largest
slides.text: The joints let the 6,800-tonne arms swing out over the water and then tilt as the gates settle to the bottom.

events.text: First automatic closure at 3 m, 21 December

slides.question: What makes the gates sink once they are across the channel?
options: Water is let into their hollow bodies
slides.explanation: The gates float out because they are hollow. Once in place, water is let inside and they submerge to the bottom of the waterway, blocking the surge.
